Karnataka’s oral epics include Manteswamy, Male Madeshwara, Junjappa and Siri Paddana. Their repertoires belong to distinct communities and local traditions, rather than one uniform statewide practice.
Folk tales form part of Karnataka’s oral prose traditions, alongside legends and myths. Storytellers share these narratives in local languages and settings.
Gaadegalu are Kannada proverbs, recognised as a concise genre of folk literature. Their meaning depends on the situation in which people use them.
Ogatugalu, or riddles, are a recognised form of Kannada folk literature. A question or description invites listeners to discover a concealed answer.
Folk songs are part of Karnataka’s wider living heritage of music, performance and craft. Repertoires are sustained through the voices of communities and their local traditions.
Sobane songs belong to local ceremonial and ritual repertoires. Research in Hassan documents women’s sobane singing associated with Somana Kunita; meanings and practices vary between communities.
Tatvapada is a Kannada song tradition concerned with spiritual and philosophical reflection. Performances use relatable language to explore questions about life and belief.
Historical recordings include grinding songs from Belagavi and transplanting and harvest songs from Sullia. They document music within agricultural and household work.
Suggi Kunitha is associated with the Halakki Vokkaliga community of Uttara Kannada. The seasonal celebration is connected with Kamana Hunnime and the farming calendar.
Somana Kunitha is a ritual performance associated with village-deity worship in parts of southern Karnataka, including Mandya, Mysuru and Hassan.
Huli Vesha, also called Pili Nalike, is associated with coastal Karnataka. Troupes perform during Navaratri and other community festivals in towns including Mangaluru and Udupi.
Channapatna is known for lacquered wooden toys and decorative objects. Workshops in the town continue a craft associated with turning, shaping and finishing wood.

Kasuti is a hand-embroidery tradition associated with Karnataka, especially the Dharwad region. Geometric arrangements and motifs drawn from architecture, animals and everyday surroundings appear on textiles.
Bidriware is a decorative metalworking tradition associated with Bidar. Its identity comes from inlaid patterns set against a darkened metal surface.
Kinnal in Koppal district is known for wooden toys and religious figures. Craftspeople known as chitragaras use lightweight wood and build up the surface before painting.
Goravara Kunitha is associated with Gorava devotees and worship of Mailara Linga. Performers combine rhythmic movement with a small hand-drum, flute and inherited songs.
Associated with the Hubballi–Dharwad region, Jaggahalige Kunitha brings large wheel-like frame drums into festive processions. Players roll and strike these instruments as the group moves.

Krishna Parijatha is a North Karnataka musical theatre tradition centred on Krishna and the parijata episode. It has its own musical and dramatic conventions and should not simply be treated as another name for Yakshagana or Sannata.

Bayalata is a broad term for open-air theatre in Karnataka. Sannata is a distinct North Karnataka folk-theatre form within this wider theatrical landscape, with song, dialogue, humour and social narratives.
Bhootha Aradhane is a living tradition of daiva worship in coastal Karnataka and Tulu Nadu. Ceremonial dress, music, oral narratives and ritual performance form part of community observances.

Nagamandala belongs to the serpent-worship traditions of coastal Karnataka. Ritual specialists perform around an elaborate serpent design made on the ground, accompanied by music and ceremonial observances.
Bengaluru Karaga is associated with the Thigala community, Draupadi worship and the Dharmaraya Swamy Temple. The flower-adorned Karaga is carried in a procession accompanied by Veerakumaras.

Gaarudi Gombe features performers moving inside large hollow puppet structures made with materials such as bamboo and papier-mâché. These figures appear at festivals and public processions, including Mysuru Dasara.

Karnataka has regional string-puppet traditions known as Sootrada Gombeyata and Yakshagana Gombeyata. Their carved wooden figures, repertories and staging reflect local theatre traditions; puppet construction varies between regions.
Hase Chittara is associated with Deewaru communities in Shivamogga and Uttara Kannada. Traditionally practised by women, its geometric designs connect with nature, agriculture and ceremonial life.
The dollu is the large drum carried by performers in Dollu Kunitha. Its resonant beats give the group a shared rhythmic foundation.
The chande is a percussion instrument heard in Yakshagana and related performance settings. Sticks strike the drumhead to produce a strong rhythmic presence.
The maddale accompanies Yakshagana and Talamaddale. The musician plays its two drumheads with the hands, shaping rhythmic phrases alongside the singer.
The tamate is a hand-held frame drum documented in Karnataka’s Old Mysuru region. Its rhythms accompany community occasions, processions and ceremonial observances.
Kamsale are paired metal percussion pieces associated with the worship of Male Mahadeshwara. Performers strike them rhythmically while singing and moving.
A small hand-drum is among the instruments carried by Gorava performers. Its sound accompanies movement, flute and inherited devotional songs.
Kinnari instruments combine a long body, strings and gourd resonators. Museum documentation identifies their use in Mysuru and South Karnataka; related forms are found elsewhere in India.
The bamboo flute is known in Kannada as kolalu or pillangovi. Flutes are among the instruments documented with Gorava performers, alongside the small hand-drum.
